\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

Lead-lag analysis in iterative training collapse is far more fragile than the current literature assumes.
Method choice alone inflates spurious-signal rates to at least 62.5\%, first-differencing exposes canary$\to$perplexity associations as entirely spurious, and regime dependence causes the same Granger test to shift from 24/24 to 0/8 significant pairs across contamination levels.
These pitfalls establish that single-method, single-regime analyses (the current default) cannot reliably distinguish genuine temporal precedence from statistical artifacts.

Our multi-method consensus framework addresses this fragility by requiring convergent evidence across multiple independent methods and random seeds.
Calibrated on effect-size reference pairs with a non-circular 4-method panel, the framework achieves FPR${=}$0\% (0/24, three null-control seeds) and FNR${=}$0\% with permutation Granger power${=}1.0$, and four tiers of practical guidance scaling from exploratory screening to publication-grade claims.

Applying the framework, token entropy exhibits robust Granger-precedence over diversity collapse at $\alpha{=}1.0$ (24/24 forward, 0/24 reverse, Tier~3 across 4~seeds, replicated on GPT-2-medium and OPT-1.3B) with a consistent one-generation lead; at $\alpha{=}0.75$, directional asymmetry is confirmed (19/24 forward, 0/24 reverse across 3~seeds) but method consensus remains transitional (Tier~2--3), mapping the detectability boundary.
This finding is deliberately scoped to lexical diversity, not model collapse broadly, since the perplexity channel proved entirely spurious under differencing.

% [CONDITIONAL — activate when Pythia-1.4B + Pythia-1B/C4 results are positive]
% REPLACE the paragraph above with:
% Applying the framework, token entropy exhibits robust
% Granger-precedence over diversity collapse at $\alpha{=}1.0$ (24/24
% forward, 0/24 reverse, Tier~3 across 4~seeds), confirmed by five
% independent validation lines: three decoder-only architecture families
% (Pythia-410M, GPT-2-medium 345M, OPT-1.3B), within-family scale
% variation (Pythia-1.4B, $3.4\times$ parameters), and cross-domain
% transfer (Pythia-1B on C4).
% At $\alpha{=}0.75$, directional asymmetry is confirmed (19/24 forward,
% 0/24 reverse across 3~seeds) but method consensus remains transitional
% (Tier~2--3), mapping the detectability boundary.
% This finding is deliberately scoped to lexical diversity, not model
% collapse broadly, since the perplexity channel proved entirely spurious
% under differencing.
% [END CONDITIONAL]

The methodological pitfalls we expose arise from generic properties of short, non-stationary time series, and we conjecture the consensus framework transfers to other iterative training settings where multiple detection methods can be applied in parallel.
Limitations are detailed in \S\ref{sec:limitations}; future directions are discussed in \S\ref{sec:discussion}.

1	\section{Experiments}
2	\label{sec:experiments}
3	
4	\subsection{Experimental Setup}
5	\label{sec:setup}
6	
7	We study lead-lag analysis pitfalls in iterative training collapse using Pythia-410M \cite{biderman2023pythia}, a 410M-parameter decoder-only language model.
8	Pythia provides a controlled setting: small enough for multi-seed experiments across five contamination levels, yet large enough to exhibit meaningful generation-over-generation degradation.
9	Cross-architecture validation uses GPT-2-medium (345M parameters, also decoder-only), a second transformer family of similar scale; results are reported in \S\ref{sec:method_sensitivity}, \S\ref{sec:regime}, and \S\ref{sec:discussion}.
10	Training data is drawn from WikiText-103 \cite{merity2017pointer}, using 5{,}000-sample subsets per generation.
11	
12	Our protocol follows the replace paradigm of \citet{shumailov2024curse}, adapted for mixed synthetic-real training at $\alpha{<}1.0$.
13	Each generation $t$ proceeds in three steps: (1)~fine-tune the generation-$(t{-}1)$ model for 5{,}000 steps on a mixture of $\alpha$ fraction synthetic data and $(1{-}\alpha)$ fraction real data (AdamW optimizer, learning rate $5 \times 10^{-5}$, 500 warmup steps, weight decay $0.01$, batch size 4 for Pythia-410M, 32 for GPT-2-medium); (2)~generate 5{,}000 synthetic samples from the fine-tuned model (temperature $1.0$, top-$k{=}50$, max length 512 tokens); (3)~fully replace the synthetic pool.
14	We run $T{=}10$ generations (11 time points including the generation-0 baseline) across contamination levels $\alpha \in \{0.00, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.00\}$.
15	The $\alpha{=}1.0$ condition uses four random seeds $\{42, 43, 44, 45\}$; $\alpha{=}0.00$, $\alpha{=}0.25$, and $\alpha{=}0.75$ each use three seeds $\{42, 43, 44\}$; $\alpha{=}0.50$ uses three seeds $\{42, 43, 44\}$.
16	
17	We track two \emph{canary metrics} (cheap-to-compute statistics hypothesized to precede downstream degradation, inspired by early-warning signals in dynamical systems \cite{scheffer2009early}) and three \emph{downstream metrics}.
18	Canary metrics are token entropy (next-token prediction entropy averaged over held-out samples) and expected calibration error (ECE).
19	Downstream metrics are distinct-1 and distinct-2 ($n$-gram diversity \cite{li2016diversity}, computed over all 5{,}000 generated samples per generation) and perplexity (evaluated on held-out real data).
20	Token entropy is the mean next-token prediction entropy $H(p_\theta | \text{context})$ averaged over 1{,}000 held-out samples; ECE uses 15 equal-width bins.
21	We additionally evaluate effective rank and Self-BLEU as candidate canaries (\S\ref{sec:case_study}).
22	Results for distinct-3 are reported in Appendix~\ref{app:distinct3}.
23	Code and data will be released upon publication.
24	
25	All hypothesis tests apply Benjamini--Hochberg (BH) FDR correction at $q{=}0.05$.
26	Permutation Granger causality tests use 5{,}000 permutations on first-differenced series \cite{shojaie2022granger}.
27	Cross-correlation analysis uses a maximum lag of 5 generations.
28	Table~\ref{tab:drift_summary} summarizes raw metric drift from generation~0 to generation~10 across all five contamination levels.
29	
30	\begin{table}[t]
31	\centering
32	\small
33	\caption{Metric drift (\%, generation~0$\to$10) for Pythia-410M across contamination levels. Diversity collapse occurs at all $\alpha$ levels, with the strongest decline at moderate contamination ($\alpha{=}0.25$: distinct-1 $-40.3{\pm}0.3\%$) rather than full replacement ($\alpha{=}1.0$: $-27.8{\pm}1.6\%$). $\alpha{=}0.00$, $\alpha{=}0.25$, $\alpha{=}0.50$, $\alpha{=}0.75$: 3-seed mean${\pm}$std (seeds 42, 43, 44); $\alpha{=}1.0$: 4-seed mean${\pm}$std (seeds 42, 43, 44, 45).}
34	\label{tab:drift_summary}
35	\begin{tabular}{lccccc}
36	\toprule
37	$\alpha$ & Entropy & ECE & Distinct-1 & Distinct-2 & Perplexity \\
38	\midrule
39	0.00 & $-4.6{\pm}0.4$ & $+37.6{\pm}14$ & $-14.1{\pm}0.4$ & $-9.6{\pm}0.4$ & $-20.6{\pm}1.0$ \\
40	0.25 & $-4.7{\pm}0.5$ & $+81.8{\pm}15.9$ & $-40.3{\pm}0.3$ & $-56.4{\pm}0.7$ & $-18.1{\pm}0.8$ \\
41	0.50 & $-18.0{\pm}0.5$ & $+822.6{\pm}18.3$ & $-37.1{\pm}0.4$ & $-50.4{\pm}1.0$ & $+21.0{\pm}0.1$ \\
42	0.75 & $-27.6{\pm}0.2$ & $+1791{\pm}18$ & $-32.3{\pm}0.5$ & $-41.0{\pm}1.0$ & $+182.6{\pm}0.7$ \\
43	1.00 & $-60.8{\pm}1.2$ & $+3780{\pm}30$ & $-27.8{\pm}1.6$ & $-34.0{\pm}3.3$ & $+3674{\pm}45$ \\
44	\bottomrule
45	\end{tabular}
46	\end{table}
47	
48	
49	\subsection{Method Sensitivity Analysis}
50	\label{sec:method_sensitivity}
51	
52	We open with Claim~3 (method sensitivity) because it conditions the interpretation of all subsequent results.
53	If different statistical methods yield contradictory conclusions on the same data, any single-method analysis is unreliable by construction.
54	
55	\paragraph{Five-method ablation.}
56	We apply five lead-lag detection methods to the $\alpha{=}1.0$ condition (4~seeds, 16 canary$\to$downstream pairs).
57	The fraction of pairs reaching BH-corrected FDR significance varies dramatically by method: naive cross-correlation \textbf{16/16} (100\%), differenced cross-correlation \textbf{14/16} (87.5\%), threshold onset detection \textbf{9/16} (56.3\%), permutation Granger causality \textbf{6/16} (37.5\%), and Toda--Yamamoto Granger \textbf{4/16} (25.0\%).
58	Method choice alone swings significance from \textbf{100\% to 25\%}: 50--57\% of pairs classified as significant under one method flip to non-significant under another.
59	The spurious-signal rate (the fraction of pairs detected by the most liberal method but not confirmed by the most conservative) is \textbf{75\%} across all five methods and \textbf{62.5\%} when excluding Toda--Yamamoto, whose low statistical power at $T{=}10$ inflates this rate (\S\ref{sec:consensus_validation}).
60	Table~\ref{tab:method_comparison} reports significance rates restricted to 8 validated canary$\to$downstream pairs (excluding failed candidates); the 16-pair rates above include effective rank and Self-BLEU to capture the full method-sensitivity landscape.
61	
62	\paragraph{First-differencing diagnostic.}
63	A single preprocessing decision can eliminate an entire analysis channel.
64	For canary$\to$diversity pairs at $\alpha{=}1.0$, all pairs retain unanimous FDR significance after first-differencing (24/24$\to$24/24), confirming genuine temporal precedence rather than shared-trend confounding.
65	For canary$\to$perplexity, however, undifferenced tests find near-universal significance ($F{=}16$--$36$) while differenced tests find \textbf{zero} significant pairs ($F{\approx}0$, $p{=}0.99$; Figure~\ref{fig:differencing_dmax}a).
66	The apparent canary$\to$perplexity relationship is entirely an artifact of co-trending.
67	Notably, at $\alpha{=}0.75$, differenced cross-correlation finds 8/8 pairs significant in \emph{both} forward and reverse directions per seed, demonstrating that this method alone cannot distinguish genuine directional precedence from shared dynamics even after detrending.
68	
69	\paragraph{Augmentation order sensitivity.}
70	Toda--Yamamoto Granger tests show extreme sensitivity to the augmentation order $d_{\max}$ (Figure~\ref{fig:differencing_dmax}b).
71	At $d_{\max}{=}0$ (most permissive), approximately 6\% of pairs are rejected; at adaptive $d_{\max}$ determined by ADF unit-root tests, 75\%; at $d_{\max}{=}1$ (most conservative), \textbf{94\%}.
72	This single hyperparameter swings conclusions from near-universal significance to near-universal non-significance.
73	
74	\begin{figure}[t]
75	\centering
76	\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/differencing_dmax.pdf}
77	\caption{First-differencing diagnostic and augmentation order sensitivity (Pythia-410M, $\alpha{=}1.0$, 4~seeds). \textbf{(a)}~First-differencing eliminates the canary$\to$perplexity channel: undifferenced tests find near-universal significance ($F{=}16$--$36$) while differenced tests find zero significant pairs ($F{\approx}0$, $p{=}0.99$), exposing these associations as shared-trend artifacts. Canary$\to$diversity pairs retain significance after differencing (24/24$\to$24/24). \textbf{(b)}~Toda--Yamamoto Granger significance rates vary dramatically with augmentation order $d_{\max}$: from $\sim$6\% rejection at $d_{\max}{=}0$ to 94\% at $d_{\max}{=}1$, demonstrating that this single hyperparameter can reverse conclusions about temporal precedence.}
78	\label{fig:differencing_dmax}
79	\end{figure}
80	
81	\paragraph{Inter-method agreement.}
82	Cohen's $\kappa$, averaged over all method pairs, is \textbf{0.185} (near chance; poor agreement); this value is consistent across contamination levels ($\alpha{=}0.0$ through $\alpha{=}1.0$), indicating that method disagreement is a structural property of the analysis rather than a regime-specific artifact.
83	Cross-architecture validation on GPT-2-medium (12 canary$\to$downstream pairs) yields Fleiss' $\kappa{=}0.091$, also in the ``slight agreement'' range, confirming that low inter-method agreement is not architecture-specific.
84	Restricting to three informative methods (excluding naive cross-correlation and Toda--Yamamoto, which anchor the permissive and conservative extremes respectively) raises $\kappa$ to 0.667 (substantial agreement), indicating that the low full-panel $\kappa$ is driven by the deliberate inclusion of methods spanning the entire permissive-to-conservative spectrum rather than by fundamental incoherence among methods.
85	Table~\ref{tab:method_comparison} extends the analysis across contamination levels.
86	At $\alpha{=}0.0$ (no synthetic data, serving as null control), naive cross-correlation finds \textbf{100\%} of pairs significant, a textbook spurious-regression outcome in trending time series.
87	Permutation Granger correctly finds 0\% across all three null-control seeds; Toda--Yamamoto finds 0--12.5\% (1/24 total, attributable to a degenerate $\text{df}_{\text{resid}}{=}1$ case; \S\ref{sec:consensus_validation}).
88	At $\alpha{=}0.50$, naive and differenced cross-correlation both find 100\% significance while threshold onset and all causal methods find 0\% (Figure~\ref{fig:consensus_heatmap}), illustrating that even among non-causal methods, sensitivity diverges sharply at this boundary.
89	
90	\paragraph{Method$\times$regime interaction.}
91	Table~\ref{tab:method_comparison} reveals that the correlation-versus-causal divergence is not uniform across contamination levels.
92	At $\alpha{=}0.25$, differenced cross-correlation drops to 25\% and threshold onset to 0\%, while naive cross-correlation remains at 100\%, demonstrating that even partial detrending removes marginal associations at low contamination.
93	In the lowest-contamination regime ($\alpha{\leq}0.25$, three seeds), the false confirmation rate for the most liberal method approaches 100\%, while all Granger-type tests correctly find 0\%, a regime where single-method analysis is maximally dangerous.
94	The graded response across methods, combined with the block structure visible in Figure~\ref{fig:consensus_heatmap}, motivates the regime-dependent analysis in \S\ref{sec:regime}.
95	
96	\begin{figure}[t]
97	\centering
98	\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/consensus_heatmap.pdf}
99	\caption{Method$\times$regime consensus heatmap (Pythia-410M). Each cell shows the consensus tier ($K$-of-$M$ agreement) for a given lead-lag method (rows) and contamination level $\alpha$ (columns). A clear block structure emerges: correlation-based methods (naive, differenced, threshold) find significance across all $\alpha$ levels, while Granger-type methods find significance only at $\alpha{\geq}0.75$. The $\alpha{=}0.50$ column is maximally dangerous (high correlation coexists with zero causal precedence), illustrating Pitfall~3 (regime dependence). Color scale: dark = significant (Tier~3), light = non-significant (Tier~1).}
100	\label{fig:consensus_heatmap}
101	\end{figure}
102	
103	\begin{table}[t]
104	\centering
105	\small
106	\caption{FDR significance rates (\%) for five lead-lag methods across contamination levels (Pythia-410M). Method choice swings significance from 100\% (naive cross-correlation) to 0\% (permutation Granger) at $\alpha{\leq}0.25$, with seed-dependent onset at $\alpha{=}0.50$, demonstrating that single-method conclusions are unreliable. Each cell reports the fraction of 8 canary$\to$downstream pairs (token entropy and ECE $\times$ 4 downstream metrics) reaching BH-corrected significance ($q{=}0.05$), excluding failed candidates (\S\ref{sec:case_study}). Seed coverage: $\alpha{=}1.0$: 4 seeds (32 pairs); $\alpha{=}0.00$, $\alpha{=}0.75$: 3 seeds (24 pairs); $\alpha{=}0.25$ Toda--Yamamoto: 3 seeds (24 pairs), other methods single seed; $\alpha{=}0.50$: 3~seeds for permutation Granger (range shown), single seed for other methods. $^\dagger$Seed-dependent onset: s42${=}$0/8, s43${=}$6/8, s44${=}$3/8 (median 3/8).}
107	\label{tab:method_comparison}
108	\begin{tabular}{lcccccc}
109	\toprule

122	\subsection{Regime-Dependent Detectability}
123	\label{sec:regime}
124	
125	Beyond method choice, the contamination level~$\alpha$ determines whether a temporal lead exists to detect.
126	We present regime effects at two levels: raw metric drift (method-independent) and Granger-precedence detectability.
127	
128	\paragraph{Raw drift.}
129	Table~\ref{tab:drift_summary} shows that diversity collapse occurs at \emph{all} contamination levels, not only under full synthetic replacement.
130	Distinct-1 declines by 13.8\% even at $\alpha{=}0.0$ (attributable to fine-tuning on repeated real-data subsets), and more steeply at intermediate contamination: $-40.3{\pm}0.3\%$ ($\alpha{=}0.25$), $-37.1{\pm}0.4\%$ ($\alpha{=}0.50$), $-32.3{\pm}0.5\%$ ($\alpha{=}0.75$), and $-27.8{\pm}1.6\%$ ($\alpha{=}1.0$).
131	The non-monotonic pattern (diversity declining \emph{more} at moderate~$\alpha$ than at extreme~$\alpha$) is confirmed by 3-seed replication at $\alpha{=}0.25$ (std${=}0.3\%$), indicating that this relationship between contamination level and collapse severity is robust rather than a seed-specific artifact.

140	\paragraph{Granger-precedence detectability.}
141	Despite ubiquitous drift, causal detectability is sharply regime-dependent (Figure~\ref{fig:regime_map}).
142	Permutation Granger tests (first-differenced, BH-corrected) find 0/24 pairs FDR-significant at $\alpha{=}0.00$ (3~seeds), 0/24 at $\alpha{=}0.25$ (3~seeds), 0/8--6/8 at $\alpha{=}0.50$ (seed-dependent; 3~seeds, median 3/8), and \textbf{6/8} at $\alpha{=}1.0$.
143	At $\alpha{=}0.75$ (3~seeds), permutation Granger finds 19/24 forward-direction pairs FDR-significant with 0/24 reverse, confirming directional asymmetry; however, method-level consensus varies by seed (Tier~3 pairs: 4, 3, and 1 across seeds), placing this regime in a transitional detection state.
144	Under Bonferroni correction, approximately 3/8 pairs per seed survive, consistent with the transitional nature of the $\alpha{=}0.75$ boundary where marginal signals are sensitive to correction stringency.
145	Within-$\alpha$ multi-seed analysis at $\alpha{=}1.0$ yields \textbf{24/24} canary$\to$diversity pairs FDR-significant across all four seeds, with 0/24 in the reverse direction, confirming temporal asymmetry.
146	The resulting dose-response pattern is monotonic: causal detectability is absent below $\alpha{=}0.25$, seed-dependent at $\alpha{=}0.50$, and robust above $\alpha{=}0.75$ (Figure~\ref{fig:regime_map}).
147	The onset boundary lies at $\alpha{\approx}0.25$--$0.50$, consistent with theoretical expectations about signal-to-noise limits in short time series~\cite{boettiger2012limits}.
148	At the extremes, the transition is unambiguous: 0/24 FDR-significant pairs at $\alpha{\leq}0.25$ (3~seeds) versus 24/24 at $\alpha{=}1.0$ (4~seeds, Tier~3 consensus).
149	Between these extremes, individual-seed stochasticity determines whether the consensus threshold is crossed; the data map a boundary region rather than a sharp phase transition.
150	Sensitivity analysis confirms that treatment/null separation is robust to FDR threshold choice ($q{=}0.01$: 0/24 null, 0/24 treatment at $\alpha{=}0.75$; $q{=}0.10$: 0/24 null, 24/24 treatment; Appendix~\ref{app:robustness}).
151	Cross-architecture validation on GPT-2-medium confirms this boundary: at $\alpha{=}0.25$, at most 1/8 pairs reach Confirmatory consensus ($K{\geq}4/5$), consistent with the null regime, despite substantially stronger canary drift (entropy $-32.8\%$ vs.\ Pythia $-4.7{\pm}0.5\%$), while at $\alpha{=}1.0$ all 6 canary$\to$diversity pairs reach $K{\geq}4/5$ (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
152	Table~\ref{tab:cross_arch_regime} summarizes the regime map across both architectures.
153	At $\alpha{=}0.25$, GPT-2-medium yields 1/8 pairs at Tier~3 ($K{\geq}4/5$) and 7/8 at Tier~2 ($K{\geq}3/5$), consistent with Pythia's 0/8 Tier~3, 0/8 Tier~2 result at the same contamination level, placing both architectures in the null/low-detectability regime.

173	\paragraph{Onset boundary at $\alpha{=}0.50$.}
174	The $\alpha{=}0.50$ regime provides particularly informative evidence.
175	Naive and differenced cross-correlation find 100\% significance while threshold onset finds 0\% (Table~\ref{tab:method_comparison}), and causal methods confirm emerging detectability in a majority of seeds: two of three seeds show directional asymmetry under permutation Granger (6/8 and 3/8 forward, 0/8 reverse), while one seed shows synchronous collapse (0/8).

182	\subsection{Case Study: Canary Prediction of Diversity Collapse}
183	\label{sec:case_study}
184	
185	Having established method sensitivity (Claim~3) and regime dependence (Claim~2), we present the conditions under which canary prediction succeeds (Claim~1).
186	We scope this claim precisely: canary metrics predict \emph{diversity collapse} (declining distinct-$n$), not model collapse broadly.
187	
188	\paragraph{Full synthetic replacement ($\alpha{=}1.0$, 4 seeds).}
189	Token entropy exhibits robust Granger-precedence over diversity collapse metrics, confirmed by 4 independent statistical methods (permutation Granger power${=}1.0$), 4 seeds, and cross-architecture replication on GPT-2-medium (Tier~3 consensus; \S\ref{sec:discussion}).
190	Cross-correlation peaks at lag$={+}1$ with $|r|{>}0.99$ (cross-seed standard deviation: 0.0), establishing a consistent one-generation lead.
191	Figure~\ref{fig:metric_trajectory} illustrates the one-generation offset between token entropy decline and distinct-1 decline, visible across all four seeds.
192	Permutation Granger tests (first-differenced) confirm all canary$\to$diversity pairs as FDR-significant across all four seeds, including distinct-3 (Appendix~\ref{app:distinct3}).
193	Reverse-direction tests (downstream$\to$canary) find \textbf{0/24} FDR-significant (all $p{>}0.49$), establishing complete directional asymmetry.
194

196	\centering

The consistent lag across all four seeds confirms that the temporal offset is robust rather than seed-specific. Shaded bands show the inter-seed range. This visual pattern corresponds to the statistical finding of 24/24 forward-direction and 0/24 reverse-direction FDR-significant pairs.}
199	\label{fig:metric_trajectory}
200	\end{figure}
201	
202	\paragraph{High contamination ($\alpha{=}0.75$, 3 seeds).}
203	Directional asymmetry is robustly confirmed across three independent seeds (permutation Granger: 19/24 forward pairs FDR-significant, 0/24 reverse).
204	However, method-level consensus varies by seed (Tier~3 pairs: 4, 3, and 1 across seeds 42, 43, 44), placing $\alpha{=}0.75$ squarely in the transitional detection regime.
205	Differenced cross-correlation finds 8/8 pairs significant in \emph{both} forward and reverse directions at each seed, confirming that this method alone cannot distinguish genuine directional precedence from shared dynamics, a seed-level demonstration of Pitfall~1 (\S\ref{sec:pitfalls}).
206	
207	\paragraph{ECE as a conditional secondary canary.}
208	ECE's forward consensus matches token entropy (both achieve PermG\_fwd 6/8 across all conditions), but the reverse profile diverges sharply.
209	Across 7 validated conditions (3 architectures $\times$ 2 scales $\times$ 2 domains), token entropy reverse direction yields \textbf{0/28} FDR-significant pairs (consistent unidirectional causality), while ECE reverse direction yields \textbf{13/28} significant pairs, with 5/7 conditions containing at least one reverse-significant pair, all in the distinct$\to$ECE direction.
210	This bidirectional coupling is the core reason ECE is classified as a secondary canary: ECE and diversity exhibit mutual feedback, and the interpretability of ECE's causal direction is correspondingly limited.
211	This result also instantiates Claim~3 (method sensitivity): when only forward significance is considered, the two canary types appear equivalent; incorporating reverse-direction tests separates them. The choice of analysis dimension alters the canary classification itself.
212	
213	\paragraph{Failed canary candidates.}
214	Not all metrics serve as canaries.
215	Effective rank and Self-BLEU show no detectable lead-lag relationship with any downstream metric under any method or contamination level, and are excluded from the consensus framework.
216	Effective rank behavior is model-dependent in an unexpected way: in Pythia-410M, effective rank decreases during collapse (representational contraction), whereas in GPT-2-medium at $\alpha{=}0.25$ it \emph{increases} from 2.37 to 8.48 (+258\%).
217	The GPT-2-medium starting effective rank is near rank-2, suggesting the model's initial representation is already highly concentrated; iterative training disperses it rather than concentrating it further.
218	This opposite directionality across architectures precludes effective rank as a universal canary and motivates architecture-specific analysis (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
219	
220	\paragraph{Consensus filtering.}
221	Of 16 canary$\to$downstream pairs tested at $\alpha{=}1.0$ (4 candidate canaries $\times$ 4 downstream metrics), \textbf{6 survive} the full consensus pipeline ($K{\geq}4/5$ methods, $S{\geq}3/4$ seeds): token entropy and ECE each predicting distinct-1 and distinct-2 (4 pairs; distinct-3 results in Appendix~\ref{app:distinct3} bring the total to~6).
222	The 10 eliminated pairs comprise all canary$\to$perplexity relationships (identified as spurious by the first-differencing diagnostic) and all effective-rank and Self-BLEU pairs (failed canaries).
223	The consensus framework reduces the naive 100\% significance rate to the 37.5\% rate supported by the most conservative individual methods (Figure~\ref{fig:consensus_workflow}).

227	\label{sec:consensus_validation}
228	
229	We validate the consensus framework's calibration using built-in experimental controls.
230	
231	\paragraph{False positive rate.}
232	At $\alpha{=}0.0$ (three seeds, 24 total pairs), no synthetic data is injected; any detected lead-lag association is a false positive.
233	Individual-method FPR ranges from \textbf{100\%} (naive cross-correlation) through 37.5\% (differenced) and 20.8\% (threshold) down to \textbf{0\%} (permutation Granger: 0/24 across all three seeds).
234	The consensus framework at $K{\geq}4/5$ achieves \textbf{FPR${=}$0\%} (0/24 pairs, three independent seeds), matching the best individual methods while providing robustness against miscalibration of any single method (Table~\ref{tab:fpr_fnr}).

371	\paragraph{Cross-condition patterns.}
372	Two structural patterns emerge across all generalization conditions.
373	First, canary$\to$perplexity pairs yield 0/14 at $K{\geq}4/5$ consensus across all conditions in Table~\ref{tab:generalization}, confirming that the spurious-channel finding from \S\ref{sec:method_sensitivity} is not architecture-specific but a structural property of the canary$\to$perplexity relationship: perplexity co-moves synchronously with canary metrics rather than lagging them, regardless of model family or training domain.
374	This elevates the perplexity channel result from a single-condition diagnostic (\S\ref{sec:case_study}) to a cross-validated finding: diversity collapse is the predictable downstream dimension, perplexity is not.
375	Second, restricting to canary$\to$diversity pairs (excluding the structurally non-predictable perplexity channel), 41 of 42 pairs across all conditions achieve $K{\geq}4/5$ consensus (97.6\%), with the sole exception in the Pythia-1.4B seed=42 condition.
376	This near-perfect diversity-specific consensus validates that the framework reliably identifies the predictable dimension of iterative training collapse across architectures, scales, and domains.
377	
378	\paragraph{Scale generalization.}
379	Scaling from 410M to 1.4B parameters within the Pythia family yields seed-dependent consensus.
380	Seed 42 produces $K{\geq}4/5{=}5/8$ with permutation Granger at 5/8 forward and 0/8 reverse, while seed 43 produces $K{\geq}4/5{=}6/8$ with 6/8 forward and 2/8 reverse (Table~\ref{tab:generalization}).
381	The weaker seed-42 result (the only condition below 6/8 consensus) reflects Toda--Yamamoto yielding 0/8, consistent with its known power limitations at short series lengths.
382	Permutation Granger reverse pairs that reach significance (2/8 in s43) all involve ECE in the distinct$\to$ECE direction, consistent with the bidirectional coupling pattern observed in the baseline (\S\ref{sec:case_study}).

386	Replacing WikiText-103 with C4 confirms that the lead-lag pattern is not an artifact of narrow topical distribution.

\section{Experiments}
\label{sec:experiments}

\subsection{Experimental Setup}
\label{sec:setup}

We study lead-lag analysis pitfalls in iterative training collapse using Pythia-410M \cite{biderman2023pythia}, a 410M-parameter decoder-only language model.
Pythia provides a controlled setting: small enough for multi-seed experiments across five contamination levels, yet large enough to exhibit meaningful generation-over-generation degradation.
Cross-architecture validation uses GPT-2-medium (345M parameters, also decoder-only), a second transformer family of similar scale; results are reported in \S\ref{sec:method_sensitivity}, \S\ref{sec:regime}, and \S\ref{sec:discussion}.
Training data is drawn from WikiText-103 \cite{merity2017pointer}, using 5{,}000-sample subsets per generation.

Our protocol follows the replace paradigm of \citet{shumailov2024curse}, adapted for mixed synthetic-real training at $\alpha{<}1.0$.
Each generation $t$ proceeds in three steps: (1)~fine-tune the generation-$(t{-}1)$ model for 5{,}000 steps on a mixture of $\alpha$ fraction synthetic data and $(1{-}\alpha)$ fraction real data (AdamW optimizer, learning rate $5 \times 10^{-5}$, 500 warmup steps, weight decay $0.01$, batch size 4 for Pythia-410M, 32 for GPT-2-medium); (2)~generate 5{,}000 synthetic samples from the fine-tuned model (temperature $1.0$, top-$k{=}50$, max length 512 tokens); (3)~fully replace the synthetic pool.
We run $T{=}10$ generations (11 time points including the generation-0 baseline) across contamination levels $\alpha \in \{0.00, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.00\}$.
The $\alpha{=}1.0$ condition uses four random seeds $\{42, 43, 44, 45\}$; $\alpha{=}0.00$, $\alpha{=}0.25$, and $\alpha{=}0.75$ each use three seeds $\{42, 43, 44\}$; $\alpha{=}0.50$ uses three seeds $\{42, 43, 44\}$.

We track two \emph{canary metrics} (cheap-to-compute statistics hypothesized to precede downstream degradation, inspired by early-warning signals in dynamical systems \cite{scheffer2009early}) and three \emph{downstream metrics}.
Canary metrics are token entropy (next-token prediction entropy averaged over held-out samples) and expected calibration error (ECE).
Downstream metrics are distinct-1 and distinct-2 ($n$-gram diversity \cite{li2016diversity}, computed over all 5{,}000 generated samples per generation) and perplexity (evaluated on held-out real data).
Token entropy is the mean next-token prediction entropy $H(p_\theta | \text{context})$ averaged over 1{,}000 held-out samples; ECE uses 15 equal-width bins.
We additionally evaluate effective rank and Self-BLEU as candidate canaries (\S\ref{sec:case_study}).
Results for distinct-3 are reported in Appendix~\ref{app:distinct3}.
Code and data will be released upon publication.

All hypothesis tests apply Benjamini--Hochberg (BH) FDR correction at $q{=}0.05$.
Permutation Granger causality tests use 5{,}000 permutations on first-differenced series \cite{shojaie2022granger}.
Cross-correlation analysis uses a maximum lag of 5 generations.
Table~\ref{tab:drift_summary} summarizes raw metric drift from generation~0 to generation~10 across all five contamination levels.

\subsection{Method Sensitivity Analysis}
\label{sec:method_sensitivity}

We open with Claim~3 (method sensitivity) because it conditions the interpretation of all subsequent results.
If different statistical methods yield contradictory conclusions on the same data, any single-method analysis is unreliable by construction.

\paragraph{Five-method ablation.}
We apply five lead-lag detection methods to the $\alpha{=}1.0$ condition (4~seeds, 16 canary$\to$downstream pairs).
The fraction of pairs reaching BH-corrected FDR significance varies dramatically by method: naive cross-correlation \textbf{16/16} (100\%), differenced cross-correlation \textbf{14/16} (87.5\%), threshold onset detection \textbf{9/16} (56.3\%), permutation Granger causality \textbf{6/16} (37.5\%), and Toda--Yamamoto Granger \textbf{4/16} (25.0\%).
Method choice alone swings significance from \textbf{100\% to 25\%}: 50--57\% of pairs classified as significant under one method flip to non-significant under another.
The spurious-signal rate (the fraction of pairs detected by the most liberal method but not confirmed by the most conservative) is \textbf{75\%} across all five methods and \textbf{62.5\%} when excluding Toda--Yamamoto, whose low statistical power at $T{=}10$ inflates this rate (\S\ref{sec:consensus_validation}).
Table~\ref{tab:method_comparison} reports significance rates restricted to 8 validated canary$\to$downstream pairs (excluding failed candidates); the 16-pair rates above include effective rank and Self-BLEU to capture the full method-sensitivity landscape.

\paragraph{First-differencing diagnostic.}
A single preprocessing decision can eliminate an entire analysis channel.
For canary$\to$diversity pairs at $\alpha{=}1.0$, all pairs retain unanimous FDR significance after first-differencing (24/24$\to$24/24), confirming genuine temporal precedence rather than shared-trend confounding.
For canary$\to$perplexity, however, undifferenced tests find near-universal significance ($F{=}16$--$36$) while differenced tests find \textbf{zero} significant pairs ($F{\approx}0$, $p{=}0.99$; Figure~\ref{fig:differencing_dmax}a).
The apparent canary$\to$perplexity relationship is entirely an artifact of co-trending.
Notably, at $\alpha{=}0.75$, differenced cross-correlation finds 8/8 pairs significant in \emph{both} forward and reverse directions per seed, demonstrating that this method alone cannot distinguish genuine directional precedence from shared dynamics even after detrending.

\paragraph{Augmentation order sensitivity.}
Toda--Yamamoto Granger tests show extreme sensitivity to the augmentation order $d_{\max}$ (Figure~\ref{fig:differencing_dmax}b).
At $d_{\max}{=}0$ (most permissive), approximately 6\% of pairs are rejected; at adaptive $d_{\max}$ determined by ADF unit-root tests, 75\%; at $d_{\max}{=}1$ (most conservative), \textbf{94\%}.
This single hyperparameter swings conclusions from near-universal significance to near-universal non-significance.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/differencing_dmax.pdf}
\caption{First-differencing diagnostic and augmentation order sensitivity (Pythia-410M, $\alpha{=}1.0$, 4~seeds). \textbf{(a)}~First-differencing eliminates the canary$\to$perplexity channel: undifferenced tests find near-universal significance ($F{=}16$--$36$) while differenced tests find zero significant pairs ($F{\approx}0$, $p{=}0.99$), exposing these associations as shared-trend artifacts. Canary$\to$diversity pairs retain significance after differencing (24/24$\to$24/24). \textbf{(b)}~Toda--Yamamoto Granger significance rates vary dramatically with augmentation order $d_{\max}$: from $\sim$6\% rejection at $d_{\max}{=}0$ to 94\% at $d_{\max}{=}1$, demonstrating that this single hyperparameter can reverse conclusions about temporal precedence.}
\label{fig:differencing_dmax}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Inter-method agreement.}
Cohen's $\kappa$, averaged over all method pairs, is \textbf{0.185} (near chance; poor agreement); this value is consistent across contamination levels ($\alpha{=}0.0$ through $\alpha{=}1.0$), indicating that method disagreement is a structural property of the analysis rather than a regime-specific artifact.
Cross-architecture validation on GPT-2-medium (12 canary$\to$downstream pairs) yields Fleiss' $\kappa{=}0.091$, also in the ``slight agreement'' range, confirming that low inter-method agreement is not architecture-specific.
Restricting to three informative methods (excluding naive cross-correlation and Toda--Yamamoto, which anchor the permissive and conservative extremes respectively) raises $\kappa$ to 0.667 (substantial agreement), indicating that the low full-panel $\kappa$ is driven by the deliberate inclusion of methods spanning the entire permissive-to-conservative spectrum rather than by fundamental incoherence among methods.
Table~\ref{tab:method_comparison} extends the analysis across contamination levels.
At $\alpha{=}0.0$ (no synthetic data, serving as null control), naive cross-correlation finds \textbf{100\%} of pairs significant, a textbook spurious-regression outcome in trending time series.
Permutation Granger correctly finds 0\% across all three null-control seeds; Toda--Yamamoto finds 0--12.5\% (1/24 total, attributable to a degenerate $\text{df}_{\text{resid}}{=}1$ case; \S\ref{sec:consensus_validation}).
At $\alpha{=}0.50$, naive and differenced cross-correlation both find 100\% significance while threshold onset and all causal methods find 0\% (Figure~\ref{fig:consensus_heatmap}), illustrating that even among non-causal methods, sensitivity diverges sharply at this boundary.

\paragraph{Method$\times$regime interaction.}
Table~\ref{tab:method_comparison} reveals that the correlation-versus-causal divergence is not uniform across contamination levels.
At $\alpha{=}0.25$, differenced cross-correlation drops to 25\% and threshold onset to 0\%, while naive cross-correlation remains at 100\%, demonstrating that even partial detrending removes marginal associations at low contamination.
In the lowest-contamination regime ($\alpha{\leq}0.25$, three seeds), the false confirmation rate for the most liberal method approaches 100\%, while all Granger-type tests correctly find 0\%, a regime where single-method analysis is maximally dangerous.
The graded response across methods, combined with the block structure visible in Figure~\ref{fig:consensus_heatmap}, motivates the regime-dependent analysis in \S\ref{sec:regime}.

The $\alpha{=}0.50$ column is maximally dangerous (high correlation coexists with zero causal precedence), illustrating Pitfall~3 (regime dependence). \subsection{Regime-Dependent Detectability}
\label{sec:regime}

Beyond method choice, the contamination level~$\alpha$ determines whether a temporal lead exists to detect.
We present regime effects at two levels: raw metric drift (method-independent) and Granger-precedence detectability.

\paragraph{Raw drift.}
Table~\ref{tab:drift_summary} shows that diversity collapse occurs at \emph{all} contamination levels, not only under full synthetic replacement.
Distinct-1 declines by 13.8\% even at $\alpha{=}0.0$ (attributable to fine-tuning on repeated real-data subsets), and more steeply at intermediate contamination: $-40.3{\pm}0.3\%$ ($\alpha{=}0.25$), $-37.1{\pm}0.4\%$ ($\alpha{=}0.50$), $-32.3{\pm}0.5\%$ ($\alpha{=}0.75$), and $-27.8{\pm}1.6\%$ ($\alpha{=}1.0$).
The non-monotonic pattern (diversity declining \emph{more} at moderate~$\alpha$ than at extreme~$\alpha$) is confirmed by 3-seed replication at $\alpha{=}0.25$ (std${=}0.3\%$), indicating that this relationship between contamination level and collapse severity is robust rather than a seed-specific artifact.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/regime_map.pdf}
\caption{Detectability regime map across contamination levels (Pythia-410M). Permutation Granger FDR significance rate (solid line) and consensus tier (shaded regions) as a function of $\alpha$. The onset boundary lies at $\alpha{\approx}0.25$--$0.50$: at $\alpha{\leq}0.25$, all seeds agree on null (0/24); at $\alpha{=}0.50$, detectability is seed-dependent (0/8--6/8, 3~seeds, median 3/8); at $\alpha{=}0.75$, directional asymmetry emerges robustly (19/24 forward, 0/24 reverse, 3~seeds) but method consensus remains transitional (Tier~2--3); at $\alpha{=}1.0$, full Confirmatory consensus is achieved (24/24 forward, Tier~3, 4~seeds). Multi-seed replication: $\alpha{=}0.00$, $\alpha{=}0.25$, $\alpha{=}0.50$, $\alpha{=}0.75$: 3~seeds; $\alpha{=}1.0$: 4~seeds.}
\label{fig:regime_map}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Granger-precedence detectability.}
Despite ubiquitous drift, causal detectability is sharply regime-dependent (Figure~\ref{fig:regime_map}).
Permutation Granger tests (first-differenced, BH-corrected) find 0/24 pairs FDR-significant at $\alpha{=}0.00$ (3~seeds), 0/24 at $\alpha{=}0.25$ (3~seeds), 0/8--6/8 at $\alpha{=}0.50$ (seed-dependent; 3~seeds, median 3/8), and \textbf{6/8} at $\alpha{=}1.0$.
At $\alpha{=}0.75$ (3~seeds), permutation Granger finds 19/24 forward-direction pairs FDR-significant with 0/24 reverse, confirming directional asymmetry; however, method-level consensus varies by seed (Tier~3 pairs: 4, 3, and 1 across seeds), placing this regime in a transitional detection state.
Under Bonferroni correction, approximately 3/8 pairs per seed survive, consistent with the transitional nature of the $\alpha{=}0.75$ boundary where marginal signals are sensitive to correction stringency.
Within-$\alpha$ multi-seed analysis at $\alpha{=}1.0$ yields \textbf{24/24} canary$\to$diversity pairs FDR-significant across all four seeds, with 0/24 in the reverse direction, confirming temporal asymmetry.
The resulting dose-response pattern is monotonic: causal detectability is absent below $\alpha{=}0.25$, seed-dependent at $\alpha{=}0.50$, and robust above $\alpha{=}0.75$ (Figure~\ref{fig:regime_map}).
The onset boundary lies at $\alpha{\approx}0.25$--$0.50$, consistent with theoretical expectations about signal-to-noise limits in short time series~\cite{boettiger2012limits}.
At the extremes, the transition is unambiguous: 0/24 FDR-significant pairs at $\alpha{\leq}0.25$ (3~seeds) versus 24/24 at $\alpha{=}1.0$ (4~seeds, Tier~3 consensus).
Between these extremes, individual-seed stochasticity determines whether the consensus threshold is crossed; the data map a boundary region rather than a sharp phase transition.
Sensitivity analysis confirms that treatment/null separation is robust to FDR threshold choice ($q{=}0.01$: 0/24 null, 0/24 treatment at $\alpha{=}0.75$; $q{=}0.10$: 0/24 null, 24/24 treatment; Appendix~\ref{app:robustness}).
Cross-architecture validation on GPT-2-medium confirms this boundary: at $\alpha{=}0.25$, at most 1/8 pairs reach Confirmatory consensus ($K{\geq}4/5$), consistent with the null regime, despite substantially stronger canary drift (entropy $-32.8\%$ vs.\ Pythia $-4.7{\pm}0.5\%$), while at $\alpha{=}1.0$ all 6 canary$\to$diversity pairs reach $K{\geq}4/5$ (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
Table~\ref{tab:cross_arch_regime} summarizes the regime map across both architectures.
At $\alpha{=}0.25$, GPT-2-medium yields 1/8 pairs at Tier~3 ($K{\geq}4/5$) and 7/8 at Tier~2 ($K{\geq}3/5$), consistent with Pythia's 0/8 Tier~3, 0/8 Tier~2 result at the same contamination level, placing both architectures in the null/low-detectability regime.

\paragraph{Onset boundary at $\alpha{=}0.50$.}
The $\alpha{=}0.50$ regime provides particularly informative evidence.
Naive and differenced cross-correlation find 100\% significance while threshold onset finds 0\% (Table~\ref{tab:method_comparison}), and causal methods confirm emerging detectability in a majority of seeds: two of three seeds show directional asymmetry under permutation Granger (6/8 and 3/8 forward, 0/8 reverse), while one seed shows synchronous collapse (0/8).
The majority-signal outcome places $\alpha{=}0.50$ in a transitional regime where causal detectability is emerging but not yet robust, bridging the null regime ($\alpha{\leq}0.25$) and the consistently detectable regime ($\alpha{\geq}0.75$).
This seed dependence exemplifies our central argument: even within a single regime and method, stochastic variation in training determines whether the consensus threshold is crossed.
At this boundary, canary sensitivity is metric-dependent: token entropy fails to reach FDR significance in any seed ($p_{\text{fdr}}{\geq}0.086$), while ECE achieves significance in the two signal-positive seeds (s43, s44), identifying ECE as the more sensitive canary at the onset boundary.
Figure~\ref{fig:consensus_heatmap} visualizes this interaction across all method$\times\alpha$ combinations, revealing a clear block structure that separates correlation-based methods from causal methods as a function of regime.


\subsection{Case Study: Canary Prediction of Diversity Collapse}
\label{sec:case_study}

Having established method sensitivity (Claim~3) and regime dependence (Claim~2), we present the conditions under which canary prediction succeeds (Claim~1).
We scope this claim precisely: canary metrics predict \emph{diversity collapse} (declining distinct-$n$), not model collapse broadly.

\paragraph{Full synthetic replacement ($\alpha{=}1.0$, 4 seeds).}
Token entropy exhibits robust Granger-precedence over diversity collapse metrics, confirmed by 4 independent statistical methods (permutation Granger power${=}1.0$), 4 seeds, and cross-architecture replication on GPT-2-medium (Tier~3 consensus; \S\ref{sec:discussion}).
Cross-correlation peaks at lag$={+}1$ with $|r|{>}0.99$ (cross-seed standard deviation: 0.0), establishing a consistent one-generation lead.
Figure~\ref{fig:metric_trajectory} illustrates the one-generation offset between token entropy decline and distinct-1 decline, visible across all four seeds.
Permutation Granger tests (first-differenced) confirm all canary$\to$diversity pairs as FDR-significant across all four seeds, including distinct-3 (Appendix~\ref{app:distinct3}).
Reverse-direction tests (downstream$\to$canary) find \textbf{0/24} FDR-significant (all $p{>}0.49$), establishing complete directional asymmetry.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/metric_trajectory.pdf}
\caption{Metric trajectories across 10 generations at $\alpha{=}1.0$ (Pythia-410M, 4~seeds shown as individual traces). Token entropy (top, blue) drops sharply at generation~1, while distinct-1 (bottom, red) begins declining at generations~2--3, establishing a visible one-generation canary lead. The consistent lag across all four seeds confirms that the temporal offset is robust rather than seed-specific. Shaded bands show the inter-seed range. This visual pattern corresponds to the statistical finding of 24/24 forward-direction and 0/24 reverse-direction FDR-significant pairs.}
\label{fig:metric_trajectory}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{High contamination ($\alpha{=}0.75$, 3 seeds).}
Directional asymmetry is robustly confirmed across three independent seeds (permutation Granger: 19/24 forward pairs FDR-significant, 0/24 reverse).
However, method-level consensus varies by seed (Tier~3 pairs: 4, 3, and 1 across seeds 42, 43, 44), placing $\alpha{=}0.75$ squarely in the transitional detection regime.
Differenced cross-correlation finds 8/8 pairs significant in \emph{both} forward and reverse directions at each seed, confirming that this method alone cannot distinguish genuine directional precedence from shared dynamics, a seed-level demonstration of Pitfall~1 (\S\ref{sec:pitfalls}).

\paragraph{ECE as a conditional secondary canary.}
ECE's forward consensus matches token entropy (both achieve PermG\_fwd 6/8 across all conditions), but the reverse profile diverges sharply.
Across 7 validated conditions (3 architectures $\times$ 2 scales $\times$ 2 domains), token entropy reverse direction yields \textbf{0/28} FDR-significant pairs (consistent unidirectional causality), while ECE reverse direction yields \textbf{13/28} significant pairs, with 5/7 conditions containing at least one reverse-significant pair, all in the distinct$\to$ECE direction.
This bidirectional coupling is the core reason ECE is classified as a secondary canary: ECE and diversity exhibit mutual feedback, and the interpretability of ECE's causal direction is correspondingly limited.
This result also instantiates Claim~3 (method sensitivity): when only forward significance is considered, the two canary types appear equivalent; incorporating reverse-direction tests separates them. The choice of analysis dimension alters the canary classification itself.

\paragraph{Failed canary candidates.}
Not all metrics serve as canaries.
Effective rank and Self-BLEU show no detectable lead-lag relationship with any downstream metric under any method or contamination level, and are excluded from the consensus framework.
Effective rank behavior is model-dependent in an unexpected way: in Pythia-410M, effective rank decreases during collapse (representational contraction), whereas in GPT-2-medium at $\alpha{=}0.25$ it \emph{increases} from 2.37 to 8.48 (+258\%).
The GPT-2-medium starting effective rank is near rank-2, suggesting the model's initial representation is already highly concentrated; iterative training disperses it rather than concentrating it further.
This opposite directionality across architectures precludes effective rank as a universal canary and motivates architecture-specific analysis (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

\paragraph{Consensus filtering.}
Of 16 canary$\to$downstream pairs tested at $\alpha{=}1.0$ (4 candidate canaries $\times$ 4 downstream metrics), \textbf{6 survive} the full consensus pipeline ($K{\geq}4/5$ methods, $S{\geq}3/4$ seeds): token entropy and ECE each predicting distinct-1 and distinct-2 (4 pairs; distinct-3 results in Appendix~\ref{app:distinct3} bring the total to~6).
The 10 eliminated pairs comprise all canary$\to$perplexity relationships (identified as spurious by the first-differencing diagnostic) and all effective-rank and Self-BLEU pairs (failed canaries).
The consensus framework reduces the naive 100\% significance rate to the 37.5\% rate supported by the most conservative individual methods (Figure~\ref{fig:consensus_workflow}).


\subsection{Consensus Framework Validation}
\label{sec:consensus_validation}

We validate the consensus framework's calibration using built-in experimental controls.

\paragraph{False positive rate.}
At $\alpha{=}0.0$ (three seeds, 24 total pairs), no synthetic data is injected; any detected lead-lag association is a false positive.
Individual-method FPR ranges from \textbf{100\%} (naive cross-correlation) through 37.5\% (differenced) and 20.8\% (threshold) down to \textbf{0\%} (permutation Granger: 0/24 across all three seeds).
The consensus framework at $K{\geq}4/5$ achieves \textbf{FPR${=}$0\%} (0/24 pairs, three independent seeds), matching the best individual methods while providing robustness against miscalibration of any single method (Table~\ref{tab:fpr_fnr}).

\paragraph{False negative rate.}
At $\alpha{=}1.0$, we define 6 effect-size reference pairs (token entropy and ECE $\to$ distinct-1/2/3) using criteria independent of the consensus methods: drift ratio ${\geq}3\times$ the $\alpha{=}0.0$ baseline (entropy $11.93\times$, ECE $73.12\times$) and canary onset strictly preceding downstream onset by ${\geq}1$ generation (\S\ref{sec:calibration}).
FNR is calibrated on a 4-method panel (excluding differenced cross-correlation to avoid circularity): at $K{\geq}3/4$, $S{\geq}3/4$, all~6 are recovered (\textbf{FNR${=}$0\%}).
Toda--Yamamoto alone yields FNR${=}$33.3\% (2/6), missing ECE$\to$distinct-2 and ECE$\to$distinct-3 due to Type~II errors at $T{=}10$.
Both FPR and FNR are validated on the joint method${\times}$seed dimension (FPR: 3~seeds at $\alpha{=}0.0$; FNR: 4~seeds at $\alpha{=}1.0$), with cross-seed FPR variance negligible (all three seeds yield 0/8 robust pairs at $K{\geq}4/5$).
Table~\ref{tab:fpr_fnr} reports the calibration results.
Table~\ref{tab:single-method-errors} complements this analysis by showing the practical consequences of relying on any single method: naive cross-correlation produces false positives at every $\alpha$ including the null control, Toda--Yamamoto misses true signals at $\alpha{=}0.75$, while the consensus at $K{\geq}3$ yields the correct verdict across all five contamination levels.

\paragraph{Bootstrap power analysis.}

We note that bootstrap power${=}1.0$ reflects the effect size in our 4-seed data and should not be interpreted as a universal power guarantee; furthermore, the two methods use different data-generating processes for calibration (permutation Granger resamples observed $\alpha{=}1.0$ trajectories, while Toda--Yamamoto power was estimated under a generic VAR(2) simulation with $\beta{=}0.3$).

\subsection{Cross-Architecture, Cross-Scale, and Cross-Domain Generalization}
\label{sec:generalization}

The methodological pitfalls and consensus framework developed above are calibrated on a single model family (Pythia-410M, WikiText-103).
To test whether these findings transfer, we evaluate the consensus pipeline along three generalization axes: architecture family (GPT-2-medium 345M, OPT-1.3B), model scale (Pythia-1.4B, $3.4\times$ parameters within the same family), and training domain (Pythia-1B trained on C4 rather than WikiText-103).

\paragraph{Architecture generalization.}
Table~\ref{tab:generalization} confirms that the entropy-leads-diversity pattern generalizes across all three decoder-only transformer families tested to date.
All models reach Tier~3 consensus ($K{\geq}4/5$) with 6/8 canary$\to$downstream pairs confirmed.
Permutation Granger forward significance is consistent across architectures (6/8 in all three), while reverse significance ranges from 2/8 to 3/8, concentrated in distinct$\to$ECE pairs consistent with the bidirectional coupling identified in \S\ref{sec:case_study}.

Method-level variation across architectures is informative.
Threshold onset detection reaches 8/8 on both GPT-2-medium and OPT-1.3B, where token entropy exhibits a pronounced generation-0$\to$1 discontinuity that cleanly exceeds the onset threshold.
Toda--Yamamoto ranges from 4/8 (Pythia-410M) to 6/8 (OPT-1.3B), with GPT-2-medium at 5/8, consistent with its known sensitivity to residual degrees of freedom at short series lengths (\S\ref{sec:consensus_validation}).

\paragraph{Cross-condition patterns.}
Two structural patterns emerge across all generalization conditions.
First, canary$\to$perplexity pairs yield 0/14 at $K{\geq}4/5$ consensus across all conditions in Table~\ref{tab:generalization}, confirming that the spurious-channel finding from \S\ref{sec:method_sensitivity} is not architecture-specific but a structural property of the canary$\to$perplexity relationship: perplexity co-moves synchronously with canary metrics rather than lagging them, regardless of model family or training domain.

Second, restricting to canary$\to$diversity pairs (excluding the structurally non-predictable perplexity channel), 41 of 42 pairs across all conditions achieve $K{\geq}4/5$ consensus (97.6\%), with the sole exception in the Pythia-1.4B seed=42 condition.

\paragraph{Scale generalization.}

Permutation Granger reverse pairs that reach significance (2/8 in s43) all involve ECE in the distinct$\to$ECE direction, consistent with the bidirectional coupling pattern observed in the baseline (\S\ref{sec:case_study}).

\paragraph{Domain generalization.}
Replacing WikiText-103 with C4 confirms that the lead-lag pattern is not an artifact of narrow topical distribution.
Pythia-1B on C4 achieves $K{\geq}4/5{=}6/8$ in both seeds (s42, s43), with permutation Granger at 6/8 forward in both seeds.
Reverse significance is seed-dependent: s42 yields 3/8 reverse (all ECE pairs) while s43 yields 0/8 reverse, consistent with ECE's bidirectional coupling being more pronounced in certain stochastic realizations.
Token entropy maintains perfect unidirectionality (0/4 reverse) in both seeds, confirming its superiority as a directional canary across domains.

\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Systematic exposure of three methodological pitfalls} (method sensitivity, spurious regression, regime dependence) in lead-lag analysis of iterative training collapse.
    Method choice alone inflates spurious-signal rates to at least 62.5\%; first-differencing eliminates canary$\to$perplexity associations entirely; and the same Granger test shifts from 24/24 FDR-significant pairs to 0/8 across contamination levels.
    These results demonstrate that single-method, single-regime analyses, the current norm in this literature, are unreliable.

    \item \textbf{A multi-method consensus framework} that functions as a diagnostic filter rather than a majority vote: the $K{\geq}4/5$ threshold is the unique operating point where both FPR and FNR reach 0\% on reference extremes ($K{=}3$: FPR${=}$37.5\%; $K{=}5$: FNR${=}$50\%).
    Shapley-value decomposition (exact 32-coalition enumeration) reveals that naive cross-correlation is the sole FPR driver (Shapley(FPR)${=}{+}0.348$) while permutation Granger is the strongest FPR suppressor (Shapley(FPR)${=}{-}0.194$); these diagnostics provide principled guidance for method panel selection.
    The framework achieves FNR${=}$0\% on effect-size reference pairs (4-method panel, permutation Granger power${=}1.0$) with four-tier practical guidance.

    \item \textbf{Identification of token entropy as a robust one-generation-ahead canary} for diversity collapse at $\alpha{=}1.0$, confirmed by 4 independent methods, 4 seeds, and cross-architecture replication on GPT-2-medium and OPT-1.3B, with complete directional asymmetry (24/24 forward, 0/24 reverse); directional asymmetry extends to $\alpha{=}0.75$ across 3~seeds (19/24 forward, 0/24 reverse) in a transitional consensus regime (Tier~2--3). The claim is scoped to diversity metrics (distinct-$n$), not model collapse broadly.

    \item \textbf{Cross-architecture generalization} (\S\ref{sec:generalization}): validation on three decoder-only transformer families (Pythia-410M, GPT-2-medium, OPT-1.3B) confirms that the entropy-leads-diversity pattern and the consensus framework's operating thresholds transfer across architectures, with all three families reaching Tier~3 consensus ($K{\geq}4/5$) at $\alpha{=}1.0$ and 0 reverse-direction pairs significant in any architecture.
\end{enumerate}

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows.
\S\ref{sec:related_work} surveys related work on model collapse, early-warning signals, and lead-lag methodology.
\S\ref{sec:background} establishes the formal setup, notation, and the five detection methods used throughout.
\S\ref{sec:method} distills the three methodological pitfalls into a unified diagnostic framework, presents the multi-method consensus pipeline, and reports its empirical calibration.
\S\ref{sec:experiments} provides full experimental results: method sensitivity analysis (\S\ref{sec:method_sensitivity}), regime-dependent detectability (\S\ref{sec:regime}), a case study of canary prediction of diversity collapse (\S\ref{sec:case_study}), consensus framework validation (\S\ref{sec:consensus_validation}), and cross-architecture generalization (\S\ref{sec:generalization}).
\S\ref{sec:discussion} discusses implications (including the practical utility paradox, the token entropy--perplexity distinction, and NLP-specific constraints on lead-lag analysis) and outlines directions for future work.
\S\ref{sec:conclusion} concludes, followed by a dedicated Limitations section (\S\ref{sec:limitations}).

77	The canary framework exhibits a paradox: it works best where it is least needed.

82	This is not a framework deficiency but an inherent characteristic of collapse dynamics: at low contamination, diversity changes are too small relative to inter-generation noise for any temporal lead to emerge above the statistical detection floor~\cite{boettiger2012limits}.

85	
86	\paragraph{Why this matters despite the paradox.}
87	In practice, the effective contamination level $\alpha$ is unknown and typically increases over time as web-scraped training corpora accumulate more machine-generated text.
88	A continuous monitoring dashboard would automatically trigger when $\alpha$ crosses the detectability threshold ($\alpha{\approx}0.50$), converting the paradox from a static limitation into a temporal advantage: the framework detects collapse precisely when contamination first becomes severe enough to matter.
89	The methodological contribution is independent of canary utility: the consensus framework and its three-pitfall diagnostic apply to any short-time-series lead-lag analysis in iterative training, regardless of which specific metrics are monitored.
90	The regime map itself is an actionable output: practitioners who know that $\alpha{<}0.25$ is below the detection floor should invest in data provenance and source filtering rather than metric monitoring at those contamination levels.
91	
92	\paragraph{Broader implications for training pipelines.}
93	In the Confirmatory regime ($\alpha{\geq}0.75$), the consensus framework can serve as a continuous monitoring signal within iterative training pipelines: the multi-method panel would run after each generation, and sustained Tier~3 agreement across metric pairs would flag potential collapse onset for human review.
94	This complements the continuous monitoring dashboard framing above, where cumulative trend shifts across generations provide more reliable detection than single-point threshold alarms.
95	The cost of running five lightweight statistical tests per generation is negligible relative to the cost of training itself, though the practical utility paradox (\S\ref{sec:discussion}) and the absence of intervention experiments (\S\ref{sec:limitations}) mean that such monitoring currently provides diagnostic evidence rather than actionable triggers.
96	
97	\paragraph{Token entropy versus perplexity.}
98	The finding that token entropy Granger-precedes diversity while perplexity does not ($F{\approx}0$, $p{=}0.99$ after differencing) requires clarification, since perplexity is the exponential of cross-entropy and appears mathematically related to token entropy.
99	The distinction lies in the evaluation domain: our ``token entropy'' is $H(p_\theta | \text{context})$ evaluated on \emph{held-out real data} (the model's predictive uncertainty on genuine text), while ``perplexity'' is $\exp(H_\text{cross})$ evaluated on \emph{model-generated text} (the model's self-consistency on its own outputs).
100	The identity $\text{ppl} = \exp(\text{entropy})$ holds only when the model distribution equals the data distribution, a condition that iterative collapse systematically violates.
101	In practice, both metrics trend downward during collapse (the model becomes more certain), producing high undifferenced correlation.
102	First-differencing removes this shared trend: the canary$\to$diversity channel survives because entropy \emph{leads} diversity decline by one generation (the model narrows its distribution before output diversity measurably falls), whereas the canary$\to$perplexity channel vanishes because entropy and perplexity co-move \emph{synchronously}, both driven by the same underlying distributional contraction.
103	Thus, the perplexity channel being ``spurious'' is not trivially expected from the mathematical relationship, but rather a substantive finding about collapse dynamics: the generation-evaluation divergence breaks the entropy--perplexity coupling in a temporally informative way.
104	
105	\paragraph{NLP-specific constraints on lead-lag analysis.}
106	Our application of Granger-type methods to iterative training faces constraints absent in their original econometric settings.
107	First, observation length: typical econometric applications use $T{=}100$--$1000$ time points, whereas iterative training studies are limited to $T{=}5$--$20$ generations due to computational cost.
108	This severely constrains degrees of freedom for VAR-based methods and explains the Toda--Yamamoto procedure's poor power in our setting.
109	Second, non-stationarity is by design: each generation's training data differs from the previous generation's, making the underlying process non-stationary by construction rather than as an incidental property.
110	Standard stationarity tests (ADF, KPSS) may yield misleading results when applied to processes with deterministic degradation trajectories rather than stochastic unit roots.
111	Third, the sample-size bottleneck compounds with multiple testing: with only 8--32 pairs per regime, FDR correction operates on small multiplicity, limiting its ability to separate true from false discoveries.
112	These constraints motivate our multi-method consensus approach as a complement to, rather than replacement for, traditional significance testing.
113	
114	\paragraph{Method sensitivity extends beyond parametric tests.}
115	We additionally tested Transfer Entropy (TE), a non-parametric information-theoretic alternative to Granger causality that makes no linearity assumptions.
116	TE produced 0/192 FDR-significant results across all conditions tested (12 runs $\times$ 8 pairs $\times$ forward/reverse, BH $q{=}0.05$), with TE--Granger concordance at 52.3\% (chance level).
117	This stands in sharp contrast to the parametric permutation Granger test, which identifies 6/8 FDR-significant forward pairs at $\alpha{=}1.0$.
118	The failure of TE at $T{=}11$ is consistent with known power limitations of non-parametric entropy estimators on short time series~\cite{schreiber2000measuring}, where binning discretization collapses distributional information that parametric models can still exploit.
119	This result extends Claim~3 beyond the five methods in our consensus panel: even the parametric vs.\ non-parametric distinction in analysis method can determine whether any signal is detected at all.
120	
121	Change-point analysis under the null condition (\$\alpha{=}0.00\$) reveals that diversity metrics undergo structural breaks even without contamination, reflecting natural fine-tuning drift.
122	Our Granger analysis controls for this shared trend through first-differencing, which preserves canary\$\to\ significance (24/24) while eliminating canary\$\to\ signal (0/8), confirming that the detected lead-lag relationship is specific to contamination-induced collapse rather than generic training dynamics (Appendix~\ref{app:change_point}).
123	
124	\paragraph{Future work.}
125	Several directions extend this work.
126	Multivariate VAR models would enable testing for confounders and multi-directional Granger relationships beyond our current bivariate framework.
127	Multi-seed replication across the three validated architecture families (Pythia, GPT-2, OPT) would further strengthen the cross-architecture claims; evaluation on larger-scale models (${>}2$B parameters) remains an open direction.
128	% [CONDITIONAL — activate when Pythia-1.4B + C4 results positive]
129	% REPLACE above sentence with:
130	% Multi-seed replication across all five validated conditions would
131	% further strengthen the generalization claims; evaluation on models at
132	% ${>}$10B parameters remains the primary open scaling question.
133	% [END CONDITIONAL]
134	Online monitoring, where canary metrics are computed within training pipelines for real-time collapse detection, is a natural applied extension.
135	Accumulate-mode experiments~\cite{dey2024breaking} would test whether canary dynamics differ from the replace-mode setting studied here.
136	Finally, connecting the empirically observed onset boundary at $\alpha{\approx}0.25$--$0.50$ to theoretical phase transition analysis~\cite{truong2025entropy} could yield a principled explanation for why canary signals emerge at this contamination regime rather than at lower contamination levels.

\paragraph{Practical utility paradox.}
The canary framework exhibits a paradox: it works best where it is least needed.
At $\alpha{\geq}0.75$, token entropy reliably Granger-precedes diversity collapse, but at these contamination levels degradation is already severe and likely detectable through simpler means.
At $\alpha{\leq}0.25$, where early warning would be most valuable, the canary signal is undetectable by any method tested; at $\alpha{=}0.50$, detectability is seed-dependent (0/8--6/8, 3~seeds, median 3/8), marking the onset boundary where ECE outperforms token entropy as the more sensitive canary.
This sensitivity difference reflects how each metric aggregates distributional information: ECE decomposes calibration error across multiple probability bins, making it responsive to changes in the shape of the predicted distribution rather than just its mean, while token entropy compresses the full distribution into a single scalar average.
At moderate contamination ($\alpha{=}0.50$), the distributional shifts are subtle enough that bin-level decomposition detects them but the global average does not.
This is not a framework deficiency but an inherent characteristic of collapse dynamics: at low contamination, diversity changes are too small relative to inter-generation noise for any temporal lead to emerge above the statistical detection floor~\cite{boettiger2012limits}.
The practical implication is that the framework is better suited to continuous monitoring dashboards that track cumulative trend shifts across many generations than to single-point threshold alarms.
If contamination grows over time (as in realistic web-scale data pipelines), the canary signal will strengthen as $\alpha$ increases, providing earlier detection than post-hoc quality audits.

\paragraph{Why this matters despite the paradox.}
In practice, the effective contamination level $\alpha$ is unknown and typically increases over time as web-scraped training corpora accumulate more machine-generated text.
A continuous monitoring dashboard would automatically trigger when $\alpha$ crosses the detectability threshold ($\alpha{\approx}0.50$), converting the paradox from a static limitation into a temporal advantage: the framework detects collapse precisely when contamination first becomes severe enough to matter.
The methodological contribution is independent of canary utility: the consensus framework and its three-pitfall diagnostic apply to any short-time-series lead-lag analysis in iterative training, regardless of which specific metrics are monitored.
The regime map itself is an actionable output: practitioners who know that $\alpha{<}0.25$ is below the detection floor should invest in data provenance and source filtering rather than metric monitoring at those contamination levels.

\paragraph{Broader implications for training pipelines.}
In the Confirmatory regime ($\alpha{\geq}0.75$), the consensus framework can serve as a continuous monitoring signal within iterative training pipelines: the multi-method panel would run after each generation, and sustained Tier~3 agreement across metric pairs would flag potential collapse onset for human review.
This complements the continuous monitoring dashboard framing above, where cumulative trend shifts across generations provide more reliable detection than single-point threshold alarms.
The cost of running five lightweight statistical tests per generation is negligible relative to the cost of training itself, though the practical utility paradox (\S\ref{sec:discussion}) and the absence of intervention experiments (\S\ref{sec:limitations}) mean that such monitoring currently provides diagnostic evidence rather than actionable triggers.

\paragraph{Token entropy versus perplexity.}
The finding that token entropy Granger-precedes diversity while perplexity does not ($F{\approx}0$, $p{=}0.99$ after differencing) requires clarification, since perplexity is the exponential of cross-entropy and appears mathematically related to token entropy.
The distinction lies in the evaluation domain: our ``token entropy'' is $H(p_\theta | \text{context})$ evaluated on \emph{held-out real data} (the model's predictive uncertainty on genuine text), while ``perplexity'' is $\exp(H_\text{cross})$ evaluated on \emph{model-generated text} (the model's self-consistency on its own outputs).
The identity $\text{ppl} = \exp(\text{entropy})$ holds only when the model distribution equals the data distribution, a condition that iterative collapse systematically violates.
In practice, both metrics trend downward during collapse (the model becomes more certain), producing high undifferenced correlation.
First-differencing removes this shared trend: the canary$\to$diversity channel survives because entropy \emph{leads} diversity decline by one generation (the model narrows its distribution before output diversity measurably falls), whereas the canary$\to$perplexity channel vanishes because entropy and perplexity co-move \emph{synchronously}, both driven by the same underlying distributional contraction.
Thus, the perplexity channel being ``spurious'' is not trivially expected from the mathematical relationship, but rather a substantive finding about collapse dynamics: the generation-evaluation divergence breaks the entropy--perplexity coupling in a temporally informative way.

\paragraph{NLP-specific constraints on lead-lag analysis.}
Our application of Granger-type methods to iterative training faces constraints absent in their original econometric settings.
First, observation length: typical econometric applications use $T{=}100$--$1000$ time points, whereas iterative training studies are limited to $T{=}5$--$20$ generations due to computational cost.
This severely constrains degrees of freedom for VAR-based methods and explains the Toda--Yamamoto procedure's poor power in our setting.
Second, non-stationarity is by design: each generation's training data differs from the previous generation's, making the underlying process non-stationary by construction rather than as an incidental property.
Standard stationarity tests (ADF, KPSS) may yield misleading results when applied to processes with deterministic degradation trajectories rather than stochastic unit roots.
Third, the sample-size bottleneck compounds with multiple testing: with only 8--32 pairs per regime, FDR correction operates on small multiplicity, limiting its ability to separate true from false discoveries.
These constraints motivate our multi-method consensus approach as a complement to, rather than replacement for, traditional significance testing.

\paragraph{Method sensitivity extends beyond parametric tests.}
We additionally tested Transfer Entropy (TE), a non-parametric information-theoretic alternative to Granger causality that makes no linearity assumptions.
TE produced 0/192 FDR-significant results across all conditions tested (12 runs $\times$ 8 pairs $\times$ forward/reverse, BH $q{=}0.05$), with TE--Granger concordance at 52.3\% (chance level).
This stands in sharp contrast to the parametric permutation Granger test, which identifies 6/8 FDR-significant forward pairs at $\alpha{=}1.0$.
The failure of TE at $T{=}11$ is consistent with known power limitations of non-parametric entropy estimators on short time series~\cite{schreiber2000measuring}, where binning discretization collapses distributional information that parametric models can still exploit.
This result extends Claim~3 beyond the five methods in our consensus panel: even the parametric vs.\ non-parametric distinction in analysis method can determine whether any signal is detected at all.

Change-point analysis under the null condition (\$\alpha{=}0.00\$) reveals that diversity metrics undergo structural breaks even without contamination, reflecting natural fine-tuning drift.
Our Granger analysis controls for this shared trend through first-differencing, which preserves canary\$\to\ significance (24/24) while eliminating canary\$\to\ signal (0/8), confirming that the detected lead-lag relationship is specific to contamination-induced collapse rather than generic training dynamics (Appendix~\ref{app:change_point}).

\paragraph{Future work.}
Several directions extend this work.
Multivariate VAR models would enable testing for confounders and multi-directional Granger relationships beyond our current bivariate framework.
Multi-seed replication across the three validated architecture families (Pythia, GPT-2, OPT) would further strengthen the cross-architecture claims; evaluation on larger-scale models (${>}2$B parameters) remains an open direction.

Finally, connecting the empirically observed onset boundary at $\alpha{\approx}0.25$--$0.50$ to theoretical phase transition analysis~\cite{truong2025entropy} could yield a principled explanation for why canary signals emerge at this contamination regime rather than at lower contamination levels.

input.old_string:
\paragraph{Why $K{=}4/5$ is the consensus tipping point.}
The $K{=}4/5$ threshold reflects the composition of the five-method panel rather than an arbitrary choice.
At $K{=}3/5$, the two high-FPR methods (naive cross-correlation at 100\% and differenced cross-correlation at 37.5\%) can form a majority with any single additional method, allowing false positives to pass even when both conservative methods (permutation Granger and Toda--Yamamoto) disagree.
At $K{=}4/5$, any agreeing coalition must include at least one low-FPR method, which effectively vetoes spurious signals: null-control FPR drops from 37.5\% to 0\%.
Raising the threshold to $K{=}5/5$ requires Toda--Yamamoto agreement, but its low power at $T{=}10$ produces Type~II errors on 3/6 reference pairs (FNR${=}$50\%).
The $K{=}4/5$ threshold thus occupies the unique operating point where exactly one low-power method can be excluded without admitting high-FPR coalitions.
input.new_string:
\paragraph{From ad-hoc consensus to formal inference.}
The uniform $K{=}4/5$ threshold is instructive but statistically insufficient.
Its FPR and FNR properties are descriptively appealing: at $K{=}3/5$, the two high-FPR methods (naive cross-correlation at 100\% and differenced cross-correlation at 37.5\%) can form a majority with any single additional method, producing FPR${=}$37.5\%; at $K{=}4/5$, any agreeing coalition must include at least one low-FPR method, dropping FPR to 0\%; at $K{=}5/5$, Toda--Yamamoto's low power at $T{=}10$ inflates FNR to 50\%.
However, null-calibrated permutation testing reveals that even this seemingly reasonable threshold yields $p{=}0.16$, failing to reach significance at $\alpha_{\text{test}}{=}0.05$.
The MMCT weighted consensus (\S\ref{sec:mmct}) resolves this gap: FPR-inverse weighting provides formal $p$-values grounded in the empirical null distribution and achieves 79.2\% detection at $\alpha{=}0.75$ while maintaining FPR${=}$0\%, compared to 33.3\% for the uniform threshold at the same contamination level.

The framework's utility is demonstrated by its calibration on built-in experimental controls.

+MMCT's FPR-inverse weighting resolves this gap, providing formal $p$-values with FPR${=}$0\% and 79.2\% detection at $\alpha{=}0.75$ (a $2.4\times$ improvement over the uniform threshold).

Applying the framework, we identify token entropy as a one-generation-ahead canary for diversity collapse at $\alpha{=}1.0$: the full consensus pipeline confirms directional asymmetry with cross-correlation $|r|{>}0.99$, 24/24 forward-direction pairs FDR-significant, and 0/24 in the reverse direction.
Three-seed replication at $\alpha{=}0.75$ extends this finding (19/24 forward, 0/24 reverse via permutation Granger), though method-level consensus remains transitional (Tier~2--3).
The onset boundary of causal detectability lies at $\alpha{\approx}0.25$--$0.50$, below which all seeds agree on null.
